1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5.strategy: Closes the centre and claims space at once, taking the f6 square away from Black's king's knight. White gets a cramping pawn and a clear space edge; Black gets a sound structure, a light-squared bishop that can still develop outside the pawn chain, and a pawn break against the base of White's chain.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5.background: For many years regarded as inferior, chiefly after Nimzowitsch, as White, was strategically outplayed by Capablanca at New York 1927. In the 21st century it became the most popular line against the Caro–Kann.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: The classical move: White develops a piece, defends e4 and prepares to recapture on e4 with the knight if Black takes it. The game stays open, with White aiming at freer development and Black relying on a sound structure and an active light-squared bishop.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3.name: Caro–Kann Defence

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2.strategy: Prepares to recapture on e4 with the knight, like 3.Nc3, but keeps the c-pawn free to support d4 and so meets a fianchetto calmly. The cost is a knight that blocks the c1-bishop, so White's development is a little less harmonious.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Modern Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2.background: Its popularity rose in the 1970s as a way to avoid Bukhuti Gurgenidze's 3...g6 against 3.Nc3.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5.strategy: Resolves the central tension at once. Black recaptures with the c-pawn and the centre becomes symmetrical, with the pawn majorities on opposite wings: White's on the queenside, Black's on the kingside. A quieter game in which White hopes for a small edge.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Exchange Variation

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn, aiming for a broad pawn centre if Black takes. The price is slowness: the pawn takes f3 from the king's knight and weakens the a7–g1 diagonal. Black can build up solidly against the dark squares or accept the challenge.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Maróczy Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3.background: Also called the Fantasy Variation and the Tartakower Variation. Alexander Morozevich, ranked second in the world in July 2008, has played it with success.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and guards d4 but does nothing for e4: after ...dxe4 the pawn attacks the knight, so White has no immediate recapture and loses time regaining the pawn. Black gets an easy game.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 with a piece, but the bishop is the one that ends up on e4 after ...dxe4, and ...Nf6 then hits it. Black develops with tempo and takes the initiative.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Be3.strategy: A gambit: after ...dxe4 White plays f3 to open lines and offers a pawn for a lead in development. The compensation is doubtful, so Black can take the pawn and defend with care.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Be3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Mieses Gambit

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Bd3 Nf6.strategy: Natural development, but it invites 4.e5 at once, which drives the knight back with a gain of space. Taking on e4 is the cleaner answer to the bishop move; this lets White into a pleasant space-gaining game.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5.strategy: Brings the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can shut it in, the main idea of the defence. White has more space, Black a solid structure and the ...c5 break against d4; the bishop is undefended on f5, which White tries to exploit.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5.strategy: Attacks the base of White's pawn chain at once. If White takes on c5, the pawn on e5 loses its support and Black can usually win the pawn back, though the light-squared bishop has a harder time getting out. A sharp, less travelled alternative to the main line.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation, Botvinnik-Carls Defence
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5.background: Named after Carl Carls, who played one of its earliest appearances at Breslau in 1912, and Mikhail Botvinnik, who relied on it in his 1961 rematch with Tal; it had remained uncommon until then. Botvinnik won the match but scored two draws and a loss with it. New in Chess also called it the Arkell–Khenkin Variation, after the work of Keith Arkell and Igor Khenkin on it.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5.strategy: The thematic recapture: it frees the c6 square for the knight and leaves Black with an easy, solid game. The centre is symmetrical, but the pawn majorities lie on opposite wings, White's on the queenside and Black's on the kingside.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn and invites White to recapture with the f-pawn, which gives White a broad centre and a half-open f-file but loosens its own king's position. A more adventurous reply than the solid ...e6: Black opens the game and challenges the centre at once.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4.strategy: Releases the tension and denies White the broad two-pawn centre and frees d5 for Black's pieces. Black gets a flexible, solid structure and a bishop that can come out before the pawns close it in.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop and pressure d4, keeping the d5 tension instead of exchanging. Black allows White to take space in the centre and on the kingside, but builds a counterattack on the long diagonal against the white centre.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Gurgenidze System
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.background: Originated by Bukhuti Gurgenidze, this variation led to a rise in the popularity of 3.Nd2 during the 1970s.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps the tension, hoping for a quiet game. White can drive the knight back with a pawn, gaining space and a closed centre for which Black may not have prepared, so Black ends up passive for little.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Campomanes Attack

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 b5.strategy: Hopes to drive the knight from c3 with ...b4, but loosens the queenside and spends a move on a pawn. White stops the idea with a3 and keeps a lead in development, so Black is left with weaknesses; it works only as a surprise at club level.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 b5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Gurgenidze Counterattack

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 dxe4.strategy: The principal answer: Black takes the e-pawn and settles the tension in the centre at once. White's knight must recapture on e4, where Black can challenge it, while Black's pawn structure stays healthy; the price is that White gets slightly more space and the first go at development.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 Qb6.strategy: Attacks the d4 pawn, which the knight on d2 has cut off from the queen. White simply defends it, and the early queen sortie has then cost Black time in the race for development without creating a lasting weakness: playable, but second-best here.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 Qb6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Edinburgh Variation

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4.strategy: Grabs the pawn with a gain of time, because the pawn on e4 attacks the knight. White has no knight that can recapture at once and must spend moves to win the pawn back; Black has to keep it defended and develop quickly for the extra pawn to count.
